exact_body_quotations.contract: The constraints are `1 <= n <= 10^4`, `n <= h <= 10^9`, and `1 <= piles[i] <= 10^9`, where `n` is the number of piles.
exact_body_quotations.rule: During each hour she eats from one pile. Finishing that pile early does not let her start another pile during the same hour.
exact_body_quotations.result: Return the smallest speed that finishes all piles in at most `h` hours.
exact_body_quotations.ceiling: For positive integers, `(p + k - 1) // k` instead gives the required upward rounding.
exact_body_quotations.rounding_proof: When `r = 0`, adding `k - 1` still leaves the quotient at `q`. When `r > 0`, `r + k - 1` lies between `k` and `2 * k - 2`, so the quotient becomes `q + 1`.
exact_body_quotations.sum: Each pile requires its own hours, so any valid schedule needs at least `T(k)` hours. Eating one pile to completion and then the next achieves exactly that total. Thus `T(k) <= h` is both necessary and sufficient for speed `k` to work.
exact_body_quotations.monotonic: Increasing `k` cannot increase the hours for any individual pile: a speed that clears it in a given number of hours can still clear it within those hours when increased. Adding the pile counts preserves that direction.
exact_body_quotations.bounds: Speed `M` clears every pile in one hour, using exactly `n` hours, which fits the guaranteed `h >= n`. No positive answer lies below `1`, and an answer exists by `M`, so start with the inclusive interval `[low, high] = [1, M]`.
exact_body_quotations.invariant: The minimum feasible speed lies in the inclusive interval [low, high], and high is feasible.
exact_body_quotations.update: Choose `mid = (low + high) // 2`, the lower middle integer. When `T(mid) > h`, set `low = mid + 1`: `mid` and every smaller speed have failed. Otherwise set `high = mid`: larger speeds are unnecessary, but the successful `mid` must remain a candidate.
exact_body_quotations.progress: When `low < high`, the lower middle satisfies `low <= mid < high`. In the failure branch the lower endpoint strictly increases; in the success branch the upper endpoint strictly decreases. The interval stays nonempty and has fewer integer candidates, so it must eventually contain one candidate.
exact_body_quotations.return_proof: The invariant then says that this sole candidate is the minimum feasible speed. Returning `low` is justified even if that exact speed was not separately tested after the final update.
exact_body_quotations.cost_model: Use a bounded-integer cost model: reading a list element, comparing these integers, and doing arithmetic on values within this problem's limits each count as constant work.
exact_body_quotations.numeric_range: Pile sizes and speeds are at most `10^9`, and an hours total is at most `n * M <= 10^13`, so their required numeric range is bounded.
exact_body_quotations.scans: The largest-pile loop visits `n` elements. A proposed speed also visits all `n` piles, performing a fixed number of arithmetic and update operations for each, so one test costs proportional to `n`. The code deliberately computes the complete total even when it already exceeds `h`.
exact_body_quotations.main_bound: Finding the maximum takes one scan. Each midpoint takes another scan, and halving the candidate range needs at most ceiling log base two of the largest pile. The total is O(n times (1 plus log M)), with constant auxiliary space under the bounded-integer model.
exact_body_quotations.space: Only a fixed number of scalars and a loop's traversal state remain live. Reassigning `hours` or an endpoint replaces its previous value; it does not retain one entry per pile or per iteration. Auxiliary space is therefore `O(1)` in the same bounded-integer model, excluding the supplied input list.
exact_body_quotations.output_space: The returned output is one integer, also `O(1)` space under this model.
exact_body_quotations.big_integer_caveat: If arbitrary-length integer inputs replaced the stated limits, arithmetic and integer storage would need a separate bit-size analysis; the scalar model here does not claim otherwise.
exact_body_quotations.ascending: If the answer is `a`, it performs `a` scans of `n` elements, or `n * a` pile visits; since `a <= M`, its worst-case time is `O(nM)`.
exact_body_quotations.ascending_worst: A single pile of size `M` with `h = 1` forces it to test every speed through `M`.
exact_body_quotations.ascending_space: Reusing the accumulator on each scan keeps auxiliary and output space `O(1)` under the same numeric model.
exact_body_quotations.ascending_min: All earlier speeds have been explicitly rejected, so its first success is minimal.
exact_body_quotations.tiny_M: If a changed task guaranteed that `M` was a tiny fixed value, ascending search would be a reasonable choice for its simpler control flow; it has no speed advantage promised here.
exact_body_quotations.pool_rule: Suppose Koko could switch piles within an hour and use the entire capacity `k` across them.
exact_body_quotations.pool_proof: In that changed task, `h` hours can consume at most `h * k` bananas, and continuously taking bananas across pile boundaries can achieve that capacity until the supply ends. Therefore `h * k >= S` is sufficient as well as necessary, and the minimum integer speed is `(S + h - 1) // h`.
exact_body_quotations.pool_cost: A single pass adds each pile to `S`, followed by a fixed amount of arithmetic: `O(n)` time, `O(1)` auxiliary space, and one integer output under the same bounded model.
exact_body_quotations.boundary: With all piles of size `1`, `M = 1` and the search loop never runs; speed `1` is already the answer.
exact_body_quotations.no_sort: These numbers are speeds, not indices into `piles`; no sorted pile list or stored list of candidates is needed.
